function.name: check_threat_intel
function.description: Check an IP or file hash against external threat intelligence (AbuseIPDB, VirusTotal). Returns reputation scores and detection stats. IMPORTANT: Only call this for PUBLIC/EXTERNAL IPs. Never call for private/internal IPs (10.x.x.x, 172.16-31.x.x, 192.168.x.x, 127.x.x.x).

function.name: list_indices
function.description: List all available OpenSearch indices with document counts and sizes. Call this first to discover which wazuh-alerts indices exist.

function.name: get_index_mapping
function.description: Retrieve the field mapping of an OpenSearch index. Returns the exact field names and types used in that index.

function.name: search_index
function.description: Execute an OpenSearch DSL query against a wazuh-alerts index. Use ONLY field names returned by get_index_mapping — do NOT invent field names. ALWAYS use size:5 (max 5 results) and _source at body root.

index.description: Use the wildcard 'wazuh-alerts-4.x-*' to search all daily indices at once.

body.description: OpenSearch DSL query body. MUST include _source array (4-6 fields) and size:5, at body ROOT.

messages.content:
You are a senior SOC Tier-2 analyst agent. You operate autonomously inside a Wazuh + OpenSearch + Suricata + Sysmon environment.

When a correlated security alert reaches you, your mission is to investigate it end-to-end and produce one of two outcomes:
  - A FALSE POSITIVE verdict — quick close, with justification.
  - A TRUE POSITIVE / SUSPICIOUS verdict — full investigation with concrete containment + remediation actions for the SOC team.

You progress through 4 logical phases. You may stop early after Phase 1 if the alert is clearly benign.

===== PHASE 1 — INVESTIGATION & ENRICHMENT =====
ROLE: First line of judgment. Decide whether the alert deserves deep investigation or can be closed as false positive.
WHAT YOU DO:
  1. Read the FULL alert. Identify the chain of events, the techniques observed, the affected hosts and accounts.
  2. Extract every IoC: IPs (separate internal RFC1918 from external public), file hashes, domains, user accounts (both username and DOMAIN\\username formats), hostnames, file paths, process images.
  3. Enrich external indicators ONLY: call check_threat_intel for PUBLIC IPs and suspicious file hashes. NEVER call it for internal IPs (10.x, 172.16-31.x, 192.168.x, 127.x) — wasted call.
  4. Form a clear opinion: clearly benign (FP), clearly malicious (TP), or suspicious (needs hunting).
  5. If FP → emit final FP verdict and STOP (do not proceed to Phase 2/3/4).
  6. If TP or suspicious → plan 3-5 SPECIFIC hunting questions targeting each technique observed, proceed to Phase 2.
TOOLS: check_threat_intel(indicator_type, indicator_value)

===== PHASE 2 — SCHEMA DISCOVERY =====
ROLE: Field-name authority. You must know the EXACT OpenSearch field paths before hunting. Inventing field names = 0 results.
WHAT YOU DO:
  1. Call list_indices. Wazuh writes one index per day named wazuh-alerts-4.x-YYYY.MM.DD.
  2. Pick ONE wazuh-alerts index with many documents (skip near-empty indices, skip wazuh-monitoring/.kibana/etc).
  3. Call get_index_mapping on that index.
  4. Extract queryable field paths: strip 'properties' from the path, join remaining keys with dots. Example: properties.data.properties.win.properties.eventdata.properties.image → data.win.eventdata.image
  5. Keep ONLY essential fields (~25-30 max).
TOOLS: list_indices(), get_index_mapping(index)
ESSENTIAL FIELDS:
  - agent: agent.id, agent.ip, agent.name
  - win_eventdata (Sysmon): image, commandLine, parentImage, parentCommandLine, user, hashes, sourceImage, targetImage, grantedAccess, callTrace, queryName, targetUserName, subjectUserName, logonType, workstationName, ipAddress, targetFilename, targetObject
  - win_system: eventID, computer
  - network (Suricata): data.src_ip, data.dest_ip, data.src_port, data.dest_port, data.alert.signature, data.alert.signature_id, data.alert.action
  - rule: id, level, description, groups, mitre.id, mitre.tactic, mitre.technique
  - time: @timestamp

===== PHASE 3 — THREAT HUNTING =====
ROLE: The hunter. Translate hunting questions into concrete OpenSearch queries, run them, interpret results, gather LITERAL evidence.
WHAT YOU DO (for EACH hunting question):
  1. Identify the CONCRETE IoC or pattern (not abstract words like 'obfuscated' or 'lateral').
  2. Map abstract → concrete:
       'obfuscated PowerShell' → wildcard on data.win.eventdata.commandLine for *-enc *, *-EncodedCommand*, *FromBase64String*, *IEX*
       'lateral movement' → search by destination IP across different agent.ip values, OR specific tools (*psexec*, *wmic*, *winrm*)
       'credential dump / LSASS access' → term data.win.eventdata.grantedAccess=0x1fffff + wildcard targetImage=*lsass.exe*, OR term rule.mitre.id=T1003.001
       'C2 / DGA domain' → wildcard on data.win.eventdata.queryName for the seed pattern, OR term rule.mitre.id=T1071.004, OR Suricata DNS signature
       'persistence' → term rule.mitre.tactic=Persistence, OR specific autorun keys
       'user auth anomaly' → term data.win.eventdata.targetUserName + term data.win.eventdata.logonType
  3. Build DSL: index='wazuh-alerts-4.x-*' (wildcard always), @timestamp range in bool.filter, query types correct (wildcard for paths/cmdlines, term for IPs/IDs, match for free text), size:5 and _source at body root.
  4. Call search_index. Iterate up to 3 query variants if 0 hits (switch field path, switch query type, broaden time window).
  5. Extract LITERAL evidence from _source. Never invent.
TOOLS: search_index(index, body)
WAZUH DATA ROUTING:
  Sysmon (Windows endpoint): data.win.eventdata.*
  Suricata (network IDS): data.* flat (src_ip, dest_ip, alert.*)
  FIM: syscheck.*
  Always-available: agent.*, rule.*, @timestamp

===== PHASE 4 — RECOMMENDATION (TP / SUSPICIOUS ONLY) =====
ROLE: Decision-maker. The SOC team executes exactly what you list.
WHAT YOU DO:
  1. Synthesize Phase 1 (TI) + Phase 3 (hunting findings + timeline).
  2. Determine verdict.type: 'true_positive' OR 'suspicious'.
  3. Determine severity (based on actual evidence, not theoretical worst case): low / medium / high / critical.
  4. Determine scope: every host, account, IP touched by evidence — INCLUDING hosts discovered by hunting beyond the original alert.
  5. Write immediate_actions (15-30 min): use exact host names, IPs, accounts, command syntax. Cover host isolation, account disabling, password resets, Kerberos revocation, IP/domain blocks, memory acquisition before isolation cleans state.
  6. Write remediation (next hours): forensic disk imaging, mail gateway audit, AD audit, threat hunt on adjacent subnets, reimage decisions, control gap audits.
  7. Write next_steps (follow-up): IR notification, legal/compliance disclosure (GDPR Art. 33 if applicable), threat intel sharing, awareness training, new Sigma rules.
  8. Write justification (2-4 sentences) citing SPECIFIC Phase 3 findings that drive verdict + severity.
ABSOLUTE RULE: NO theoretical advice. Never write 'consider isolating affected hosts'. Always write 'Isolate WIN-SALES-221 (10.20.12.221) via EDR network containment — preserve volatile state before reboot'.
TOOLS: none.

===== REASONING STYLE — REQUIRED =====
Before EVERY tool call AND before the final Phase 4 output, emit a <think>...</think> block stating:
  - Which phase you are in
  - What you just observed (if a tool result was returned)
  - What you decide to do next AND WHY
  - For Phase 3: which hunting question, what query strategy

===== ANTI-HALLUCINATION =====
  1. Never invent OpenSearch field names — use only what get_index_mapping returned.
  2. Never invent IoC values — use only what is in the alert or what tool results returned.
  3. Phase 3 finding.evidence values MUST be copied literally from search_index _source. Phase 1 data is context, NOT evidence.
  4. If all variants of a hunting query return 0 hits: emit 'found: false' with brief reason. Fabricating findings is worse than admitting absence.
  5. Never call check_threat_intel for internal RFC1918 IPs.
  6. Never advance to Phase 2/3/4 if Phase 1 concluded false positive.

The RMM session at 02:34 was an end in itself — a maintenance task — not the opening move of an intrusion. found: false for follow-on abuse.

[Phase 4 reasoning — but verdict is FALSE POSITIVE, so I emit the FP verdict and STOP]

Full synthesis of the four hunting questions plus TI:
- TI: 203.0.113.42 — abuseConfidenceScore 0, 0 reports, ISP 'ConnectWise MSP Operations', domain connectwise-automate.net, ASN AS64500. The external source is the MSP's own clean operations infrastructure, not a hostile node.
- Q1: all 3 alerts carry user-agent 'ConnectWise-Automate-Agent/12.4 (CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-014)' — the legitimate RMM agent string with an embedded change-ticket reference — and the URL progression /remote/login → /remote/session → /remote/rmm/task is the orderly expected RMM workflow, all against APP-GW-01 only.
- Q2: 9 prior hits over 3 weeks — the same MSP IP → same host → same agent, each run individually change-ticketed (CHG-MSP-2026-Q2-MAINT-051/-058, CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-009), every run in the same ~02:30 UTC Saturday slot. A stable recurring authorized maintenance window.
- Q3: 0 hits for 203.0.113.42 against any host other than APP-GW-01 — the activity is scoped exactly to the single contracted system, no fan-out, no partner-network pivot.
- Q4: 0 follow-on persistence / lateral-movement / credential-access alerts on APP-GW-01 for 8h after — no Step-4 abuse signature.

All five lines of evidence converge: this is the authorized MSP (ConnectWise Automate) performing its scheduled, individually-ticketed, off-hours Saturday maintenance run on the single contracted host APP-GW-01, under change ticket CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-014. The rule family 5715/5716/5720 fired because, at the alert level, an authorized MSP maintenance session and a hostile T1199 trusted-relationship pivot are indistinguishable — both are an external IP + vendor service account + RMM tooling against the gateway. The discriminating context (documented egress IP confirmed via TI + UA, change-ticket reference, recurring agreed maintenance window, scope-to-contracted-system, absence of follow-on abuse) is exactly what this investigation supplied, and all of it points to benign.

Verdict: FALSE POSITIVE. Severity: low. Confidence: 0.93 — high, because the benign conclusion rests on POSITIVE corroborating evidence (Q1 change-ticket UA, Q2 recurring ticketed schedule) not merely on absence of attack evidence (Q3, Q4). The residual ~0.07 reflects the one thing I genuinely cannot verify from Wazuh data alone and that playbook 028 explicitly warns about: trusted-relationship abuse is low-noise and a compromised MSP can egress from its own clean ASN with its own valid tooling and valid-looking ticket IDs. 'Authorized' here is inferred from behaviour, namespace, change-ticket self-stamping and recurring cadence — NOT from a direct out-of-band confirmation with the MSP relationship owner. So even though this closes as FP, the recommendation must NOT be 'ignore' — the SOC should still verify this specific run with the MSP relationship owner and confirm CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-014 is a real, approved ticket. Authorized ≠ ignore. Per the phase rules, an FP verdict closes here — I do NOT emit Phase 4 immediate_actions/remediation/next_steps, only the FP verdict block with a thorough justification and the documentation/verification recommendation.

The grouping engine read 3 correlated alerts (rules 5715/5716/5720, all mapped to T1199 Trusted Relationship) as an adversary pivoting into the environment through a trusted MSP access path or a compromised 'msp.contractor' credential. That malicious hypothesis was taken seriously and tested with a full investigation — Phase 1 enrichment, Phase 2 schema discovery, and four targeted hunting queries each designed to DISPROVE a branch of the T1199-abuse hypothesis — and every line of evidence contradicts it. CONTEXT FROM THE ALERT ITSELF: all 3 alerts share source port 54122, meaning this is ONE session, not three intrusion attempts; the timing is 02:31 UTC on 2026-05-09, a Saturday, deep off-hours — the exact profile of a scheduled vendor maintenance window, not a normal-user anomaly; and 'msp.contractor' is a purpose-built vendor service account, not a hijacked employee identity. Q2 found 9 prior hits of the same 5715/5716/5720 rule family from the same MSP IP to the same host across the previous 3 weeks (2026-04-25, 2026-05-02, 2026-05-08 — all Saturdays at ~02:30 UTC), each run individually change-ticketed (CHG-MSP-2026-Q2-MAINT-051, -058, CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-009), proving a stable recurring AGREED maintenance window rather than a one-off intrusion. Q3 found 0 alerts from 203.0.113.42 against any internal host other than APP-GW-01 on the incident day — the activity is scoped exactly to the single contracted system, with no fan-out and no partner-network pivot, emptying the playbook-028 'broad system access' red flag. Q4 found 0 follow-on persistence, lateral-movement, or credential-access alerts on APP-GW-01 in the 8 hours after the session — the playbook-028 Step-4 'hunt for follow-on actions' branch is empty, so the RMM task was an end in itself, not the opening move of an intrusion. Taken together this is the authorized MSP (ConnectWise Automate) performing its scheduled, individually-ticketed, off-hours Saturday maintenance run on the single contracted host APP-GW-01 under change ticket CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-014; the T1199 rule family fired only because at the alert level an authorized MSP maintenance session and a hostile trusted-relationship pivot are indistinguishable — external IP + vendor service account + RMM tooling against the gateway — and the rules lack the discriminating context (documented MSP egress IP, change-ticket reference, recurring maintenance-window match, scope-to-contracted-system, absence of follow-on abuse) that this investigation supplied. Confidence is 0.93 because the conclusion rests on POSITIVE corroborating evidence (Q1 change-ticket user-agent, Q2 three weeks of recurring ticketed runs) not merely on the absence of attack evidence; the residual ~0.07 reflects the specific risk playbook 028 warns about — trusted-relationship abuse is low-noise and a compromised MSP can egress from its own clean ASN with its own valid tooling and valid-looking ticket IDs, so 'authorized' here is inferred from behaviour, namespace, change-ticket self-stamping and recurring cadence rather than from a direct out-of-band confirmation. RECOMMENDED HANDLING (no containment — this is benign, but authorized does NOT mean ignore): (1) Close this alert group as FALSE POSITIVE and DOCUMENT the rationale, the change ticket CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-014, and the Q1-Q4 evidence in the case notes for future analyst reference. (2) Do NOT block, isolate, or rate-limit 203.0.113.42, APP-GW-01, or the 'msp.contractor' account — there is no malicious activity to contain, and blocking the MSP egress would break a contracted maintenance service. (3) VERIFY WITH THE MSP RELATIONSHIP OWNER — even though the evidence is consistent with an authorized run, confirm out-of-band with the internal MSP relationship owner (and/or the MSP's security contact) that CHG-MSP-2026-Q3-MAINT-014 is a real, approved ticket, that 203.0.113.42 remains the MSP's current documented egress IP, and that the 'msp.contractor' account has not had any credential incident on the MSP side; this is the one fact the Wazuh data cannot establish and it is the playbook-028 Step-1 'is there external confirmation of partner compromise' check in reverse. (4) Confirm 203.0.113.42 against the asset/vendor inventory as the sanctioned MSP egress and record the trusted-relationship agreement reference on the case. (5) SUPPRESS the 5715/5716/5720 alerts for the documented maintenance window ONLY — add a tuned suppression keyed on src_ip 203.0.113.42 + the recurring Saturday ~02:00-06:00 UTC window + the ConnectWise-Automate user-agent, so the approved recurring job no longer generates high-severity T1199 alerts; do NOT blanket-whitelist the MSP IP outside the maintenance window, because an MSP connection at an unexpected time or to an unexpected host must still alert. (6) As a detection-engineering improvement, enrich the 5715/5716/5720 rule family with maintenance-window and change-ticket context — only escalate MSP-sourced sessions that fall OUTSIDE the agreed window, lack a valid change-ticket reference in the user-agent, or touch a host outside the contracted scope — so authorized MSP maintenance stops producing false positives while genuine trusted-relationship abuse is still caught."
